newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldovan parliament chief boosts presidential bid.
newsitem.headline: Moldovan parliament chief boosts presidential bid.

text.p: Moldova's parliamentary chief bolstered his chances on Tuesday of ousting President Mircea Snegur in next month's election runoff by wooing the prime minister of the former Soviet republic into his camp.
Petru Lucinschi, who trailed Snegur by 11 points in Sunday's first round, might also pick up the support of communists, who regard Snegur as an autocrat.
Snegur says Luchinschi, who won 28 percent of votes on Sunday, would take the small wine-growing country of 4.3 million back to Soviet-style communism.
"Moldova is in danger...We must set up a joint front against communist and revanchist forces from the left," Snegur, the first-round winner with 39 percent of votes, said on Tuesday.
"Who is a greater destroyer of Moldova's democracy than Lucinschi?" he told a news conference.
Despite Snegur's call for unity, it was still unclear whether nationalist Valeriu Matei, who got nine percent of votes in last Sunday's first round, would back the president.
"The issue has to be discussed with my party on Sunday," Matei said.
Lucinschi said on Tuesday he had won the endorsement of Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, who trailed with nine percent on Sunday.
One of his aides said the communists, whose leader Vladimir Voronin got 10 percent, were also likely to back the parliamentary chairman in the runoff.
The other four candidates got two percent of votes or less.
Analysts say Snegur and Lucinschi are likely to attract forces roughly equal in numbers and influence and find it hard to predict the outcome of the runoff.
The two candidates' heated campaigns have been overshadowed by mudslinging and telephone-tapping.
Centre-right Snegur and left-leaning Lucinschi offer two different scenarios for the mainly agricultural land, which is sandwiched between Romania and Ukraine.
Snegur, 56, a senior communist party apparatchik in the past, wants closer ties with the West and Romania with which Moldova shares a common language, history and culture.
The tall, bulky president has cultivated the image of a strongman and "one of us", talking in his meet-the-people chats about the "corrupt" government and parliament.
He says that if reelected, he would disolve both bodies and change the constitution to turn Moldova into a presidential republic.
Lucinschi, a bespectacled intellectual and also 56, presents himself as a moderate politician whose credo is European social democracy and equally close ties with East and West.

A former top communist party leader in Soviet Moldova, Lucinschi promises to settle a dispute with pro-Russian separatists in the rebel Dnestr region who broke away on fears that Moldova might try to merge with Romania.
Lucinschi calls Snegur's demands for greater presidential powers unconstitutional and plays up his "good personal relations" with leaders of Russia, Moldova's prime supplier of fuel and energy.

Calling Lucinschi and his leftist backers neo-communists, Snegur said on Tuesday: "They want to turn Moldova backwards and direct it only towards the East. This would happen in a week after Lucinschi won power, believe me."
But Lucinschi thinks the choice between him and Snegur is not that complicated.
"Now there are two (former) communists -- Snegur and Luchinschi -- and it is up to people to decide which of them is better or more democratic," he told a news conference on Monday.
